preamble: Close [u] is laxed to near-close [ʊ], usually as a short or closed-syllable variant. In English, short Middle English /u/ became lax /ʊ/ (pullen /ˈpulən/ > pull /pʊl/), and long /uː/ from the Great Vowel Shift was later shortened to /ʊ/ in good and foot. In Javanese /u/ is [ʊ] in closed syllables (kuru [kuru] 'thin', mung [mʊŋ] 'only'). In Bashkir, Proto-Turkic *u became the reduced [ʊ̞] (*kum > ҡом [qʊ̞m] 'sand'), where Tatar has the reduced mid [ŏ]. In Turkish, /u/ is lowered to [ʊ] in the final open syllable of a phrase (uyku [ujˈkʰʊ] 'sleep').

examples.note: Roger Lass dates the laxing of short /u/ to /ʊ/ to the 17th century; other scholars date it earlier. Where /ʊ/ was not protected by a neighbouring labial or a following /l ʃ tʃ/ it later unrounded to /ʌ/ (FOOT–STRUT split).

examples.from: Early Modern English good /uː/ (< Middle English /oː/)
Early Modern English foot /uː/ (< Middle English /oː/)
examples.note: A later shortening of /uː/ to /ʊ/ in a handful of words; earlier-shortened blood and flood went on to /ʌ/.

Western Javanese keeps [u] and Eastern Javanese has [ɔ] in closed final syllables. This follows the six-vowel analysis of Javanese, in which [ʊ] is an allophone of /u/; Wiktionary writes it inside phonemic slashes.

Proto-Turkic *u became the reduced vowel spelled о, written [ʊ̞] by Wiktionary and /qʊm/ in Wikipedia's table. Wikipedia matches the Bashkir reduced vowels with Kazakh ones (Kazakh ұн /ʊ̆n/, Bashkir он /ʊ̆n/ 'flour'). Tatar о, from the same *u, is the reduced mid [ŏ] (u → o).

languageExamples.context: Final open syllable of a phrase

examples.note: Wikipedia: /i, y, u, e, œ/ are lowered to [ɪ, ʏ, ʊ, ɛ, œ] in the final open syllable of a phrase (Zimmer & Orgun) or word-finally (Göksel & Kerslake, as cited by Wikipedia).
Only the final /u/ is lowered; the first stays [u].
